title: What Happens When AI Agents Make Contracts? Bridget McCormack on LCP — full episode transcript
pub: AI and the Future of Law / 2030 Vision, American Arbitration Association
author: Jen Leonard · Bridget McCormack

st.t: Production model: Institutional absorption governs AI value
st.an: The source extends the cluster’s institutional-absorption thesis into AI-agent commerce: lawyers would adapt legal infrastructure for machine-mediated markets, including making authoritative legal statements agent-readable. It also supports the cluster’s qualified labour outlook by predicting new legal work rather than straightforward lawyer substitution, though these remain exploratory proposals rather than empirical findings.
qs: So taking the legal infrastructure that has served humans in markets for thousands of years and building it into what is going to be a larger commercial market is a really interesting set of problems.
But probably the ALI needs to figure out how to make sure agents can read the statements.

st.t: Professional engagement: Lawyers should shape AI deployment
st.an: The source accepts the engagement-first proposition and materially develops its governance dimension by calling on general counsel involved in agentic commerce to contribute to the LCP and help formulate further procedural and substantive standards. It remains a recommendation rather than evidence that such participation will produce effective governance.
qs: But if you’re the general counsel at a business that’s going to be involved in agentic commerce, get involved in the LCP and contribute to it.
And maybe start thinking about what else we might want to build—what other legal principles, procedural or substantive, we might want to think about building into future standards.

st.t: Service redesign: Resistance reflects incentives and identity
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s framing of AI as a redesign challenge rather than a software purchase and materially extends it to agent-mediated commerce. It proposes preventive legal infrastructure, inventories of agent involvement, contract redesign, protocol monitoring and machine-readable legal principles. These are practical recommendations and predictions, not evidence of demonstrated transformation effects.
qs: In commercial transactions, we’re talking about money—not air traffic control, not planes going down—but still, it will be a significant impediment to the success of the market if the legal infrastructure isn’t thought through at the front end.
Bridget McCormack: I guess the one thing I would say is to make sure you have an inventory of where agents are already touching transactions.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source reinforces the need for selective, risk-based deployment and materially extends it to agentic commerce and evidentiary integrity. It identifies concrete operating-model responses—document authentication safeguards, specialist recruitment, training for neutrals and buyer-side participation in standards—while acknowledging that agents’ comparative error rates remain unknown.

Are there going to be new evidentiary issues we should be thinking about and maybe training our neutrals to be prepared for?

st.t: Everyday usability: Better formats do not prove accuracy
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s account of practical, human-directed AI assistance: integrated workflows can improve convenience, while attractive slide output remains constrained by editing and formatting failures. Its Manus example specifically reinforces that results can depend on precise instructions rather than general style-matching requests, without establishing broader accuracy or comparative performance.
qs: But for a while, when you did decks in NotebookLM, the illustrations were amazing and everything looked great, but you couldn’t really change it around.
So I went into Canva and copied the exact color that we used in the last deck—all the numbers—and took a screenshot and uploaded it to Manus.

kp.k: Agentic commerce exposes gaps in existing contractual infrastructure
kp.d: McCormack argues that agents increasingly negotiate and form contracts, including more complex transactions, while click-through terms and other infrastructure developed for human e-commerce may not translate. She describes payment firms, banks, frontier model companies and retailers as advancing this market largely without the legal industry. This is her diagnosis of an emerging infrastructure problem, not a measured finding about adoption or enforceability.
qs: Agents are forming contracts with agents.

all of the legal infrastructure that has supported e-commerce over the last 20 years kind of grew up around e-commerce—click-through terms, terms of service before you hit the next page—and none of that necessarily translates, and maybe not at all, to when agents are negotiating contracts with agents.
And I do think the commerce market is moving incredibly quickly, in large part because it has been moving without the legal industry for now.

kp.k: LCP makes contractual terms discoverable and preserves transaction records
kp.d: McCormack describes Legal Context Protocol, developed with David Fisher, as infrastructure enabling transacting agents to locate basic legal terms at a known location and preserve the agreed terms with payment through hashing. More complex terms can be added. Its stated purpose is to establish a durable record for subsequent disputes, rather than resolve every legal issue arising from agentic commerce.
qs: the basic legal terms of the contract—what was consented to, what was agreed to—need to be findable at a known location, verifiable by the agents that are transacting, and then hashable with the payment so that if there is a dispute later, there is a single source of truth about what was agreed to and what legal terms governed the agreement.
I’m not saying it will solve every legal problem in this new market, but it will be a big step forward.

kp.k: Dispute resolution clauses remain optional under LCP
kp.d: McCormack corrects Leonard’s suggestion that LCP necessarily specifies how disputes will be resolved. Sellers may include dispute resolution provisions, but the protocol does not require them. She identifies discoverable terms and hashing those terms with payment as the agreed minimum, while acknowledging that performance, authority and other issues can remain contested.
qs: If a seller in an agentic commerce market wants a dispute resolution provision in their findable legal terms at the LCP well-known URL, they can have that. But you don’t have to.
the basic terms that are agreed to—whether they are only basic terms or whether there are more—are hashed and stored with the payment.

There might be a question about performance. There might be a question about authority. There might be lots of questions. But there should not be a question about the specific legal terms that were agreed to at the time.

kp.k: LCP separates contractual infrastructure from model reliability
kp.d: McCormack explicitly distinguishes LCP’s function from correcting generative AI mistakes. Its design is agnostic about comparative or future model quality and does not prevent an agent from inventing authority or other important information. Machine-readable, discoverable and permanent contractual terms are a separate concern from whether the AI acts correctly.
qs: LCP is totally agnostic on how good AI is, and how good your AI is versus your counterparty’s AI, and how good your AI is today versus your AI 12 months from now.
So the agent may hallucinate authority or hallucinate something important. That’s not a problem that LCP is solving at all. That’s an AI problem.
When you’re thinking about what LCP can do, it does not attempt to make up for any inadequacy in any particular AI model used in an agentic commercial transaction.

kp.k: Protocol governance is open, interoperable and still developing
kp.d: McCormack describes LCP as technology agnostic, Apache 2.0 licensed and interoperable with other protocols, with AAA and Integra Ledger co-stewarding it. Community agreement on minimum terms, wider participation and eventual donation to the Linux Foundation are described as expectations or goals, not completed governance outcomes. She presents it as a noncommercial protocol rather than a proprietary legal product.
qs: It’s technology agnostic. It’s Apache 2.0 licensed. It integrates with every other protocol so that it’s totally interoperable.
We’re co-stewarding it with Integra Ledger, but there will be lots of others contributing to it and others on the steering committee.
The goal is, like with the others, to eventually donate it to the Linux Foundation—which is apparently how this goes.
It will be completely open to all contributors to figure out how far the community wants LCP to go.

kp.k: AAA positions itself as a neutral infrastructure convener
kp.d: McCormack argues that AAA’s nonprofit status, absence of a commercial stake in transaction volume and dispute-resolution experience make it suited to convening protocol development. She reports that AAA has administered over 9 million disputes since 1926 and that in-house teams at payments and technology companies have welcomed its organizing role. These are institutional claims and reported reactions, not independent assessments of neutrality or market acceptance.
qs: The AAA has been administering disputes that have been resolved since 1926—over 9 million disputes.
I think not having a commercial stake in transaction volume makes us, in some ways, the perfect convener.

David and I have done a lot of meetings with in-house teams at payments companies and other tech companies that are in the market, and they seem pretty delighted that the AAA is willing to play this organizing role.

kp.k: Agentic disputes require new expertise and potentially new services
kp.d: McCormack expects disputes even if agents ultimately make fewer mistakes than humans; she expressly leaves comparative error frequency and impact uncertain. She reports AAA is working on new dispute-resolution expertise and raises panel recruitment, evidentiary issues and neutral education as preparation questions. New dispute-resolution options are a possibility, with AI itself supplying tools to build them.
qs: They may make fewer mistakes than humans. They may make more mistakes than humans. They may make less impactful mistakes than humans or more impactful mistakes than humans. It’s hard to know.

Do we need to recruit new people to our panel? Are there going to be new evidentiary issues we should be thinking about and maybe training our neutrals to be prepared for? What education do our neutrals need?
It’s not only that we will need new dispute resolution expertise. We will. And we’re working on that.
We may even need new dispute resolution options, which is exciting for us because we like to build new dispute resolution options, and AI gives us the tools to do that.

kp.k: Procurement hypothetical illustrates scaled exposure and ratification risks
kp.d: McCormack recounts a hypothetical from her paper with Dave Hoffman: a mid-sized industrial manufacturer’s misconfigured procurement agent accepts broad supplier-favoring indemnification terms and completes 12,000 transactions across hundreds of suppliers over a weekend. She describes subsequent acceptance of goods and payment of invoices as completing ratification on most deals despite no human reading the terms. This is an illustrative doctrinal scenario, not an observed incident or judicial holding; she uses it to argue for clear records of terms and agent authority to simplify litigation.
qs: As a result of a configuration error, there is a problem where the agent accepts counterparty terms that include a broad indemnification clause running in the supplier’s favor.
Over the weekend, the agent completes 12,000 transactions across hundreds of suppliers.
By the time everyone notices, ratification is already complete on most of those deals. The company has accepted the benefits with notice of the terms, even though no human ever read them.

And the question will be whether the company has a record that is clear, so that it can litigate those issues efficiently, or whether the terms and what went wrong are impossible to find and turn into decades-long litigation where everybody is trying to figure it out.

kp.k: Agentic commerce creates prospective advisory work for lawyers
kp.d: McCormack predicts new legal work designing the infrastructure of agent-mediated commerce, countering claims that AI will eliminate the need for lawyers. She advocates involvement before problems occur and explores making procedural and substantive legal principles machine-readable, including ALI statements. These are opportunities and proposed extensions beyond LCP, not demonstrated employment growth.
qs: I do think there is some really, really interesting work for lawyers coming as a result of this future market. It is exactly the opposite of, “Oh gosh, no one’s going to need lawyers anymore.”
But probably the ALI needs to figure out how to make sure agents can read the statements. I think that’s the next step.
And this is a moment for lawyers who want to be involved in the creativity at the front end of: what could we do to support all of this new commercial activity?

kp.k: Counsel should inventory agents and revise contractual assumptions
kp.d: For general counsel and law firm partners, McCormack recommends identifying where agents already touch transactions, including procurement, customer service and marketing; checking whether form contracts address machine-mediated formation and performance; and monitoring payment and connectivity protocols. She urges general counsel involved in agentic commerce to contribute to LCP and consider additional legal standards. Her suggestion that most existing forms do not contemplate such activity is not supported by a contract survey in the transcript.
qs: make sure you have an inventory of where agents are already touching transactions.
Then I would look at your form contracts and see whether they contemplate machine-mediated formation and performance. Most probably don’t. And some of those might fail in surprising ways.
But if you’re the general counsel at a business that’s going to be involved in agentic commerce, get involved in the LCP and contribute to it.
The LCP is only an opener. There’s a lot more we can do.

kp.k: Synthetic documents motivate provenance safeguards in legal practice
kp.d: McCormack regards AI-generated fake documents as particularly concerning because documentary evidence appears in nearly every dispute. She recommends lawyers consider hashing documents to establish a reference point if authenticity is later contested. She also reports that AAA offers Integra services for hashing arbitration-related agreements or other documents; her assessment of synthetic-document effectiveness is qualitative.
qs: There aren’t that many disputes that turn on a video or an audio file, but almost all of them turn on some document.
AI has made deepfake documents unbelievably effective and simple.
So it may be time for lawyers to figure out how to hash documents so that if there is a debate later about whether a particular one is the correct one, they have some single point of truth.

kp.k: Everyday AI use illustrates integration and uneven task performance
kp.d: The hosts offer personal usage anecdotes rather than comparative evaluations: McCormack reports Claude obtaining phone permissions and sending emails within the same app; Leonard describes recurring AI news roundups and better success reproducing slide colors in Manus than Claude. These examples illustrate expanding workflow execution alongside task-specific limitations, without establishing legal-work productivity gains.
qs: I asked Claude to do that, and sure enough, Claude just asked me for the right permissions on my phone and sent me an email with the information I asked for.
Doing all the things in one app instead of switching between apps.
Claude could not do it. I copied and pasted the number into Claude, and it was giving me this teal color. I really needed a lime green color.
Manus was able to do it.
I’ve been doing a weekly roundup of news related to AI and the legal profession and AI generally. On Monday mornings, when I log in, it’s available to me and I can review it.

kp.k: Cybersecurity discussion distinguishes reported capabilities from feared consequences
kp.d: Leonard reports that Anthropic restricted Mythos release after testing revealed strong vulnerability-discovery capabilities, including vulnerabilities in 30-year-old systems. She attributes a six-to-18-month catch-up estimate to Dario Amodei and separately predicts another usable model within 12 months. The hosts discuss potentially severe infrastructure attacks and possible regulatory or international cooperation responses, but provide no test results; these are reported developments, forecasts and speculative scenarios rather than established outcomes.
qs: during testing, they realized that Mythos is really, really effective at finding software vulnerabilities—latent software vulnerabilities that some of the most advanced cybersecurity experts would never find, sometimes in 30-year-old systems where the vulnerabilities had never been disclosed before.
Anthropic decided it was too dangerous for public release.
I think Dario Amodei suggested it would be between six and 18 months from now that one of these other labs will have this capacity.

It just seems like the speed at which these labs release new models without fully understanding what their capabilities are suggests to me that there will probably be a model in the next 12 months from somebody that people will be able to use for this purpose.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: McCormack claims AI makes document fabrication easier and more convincing, creating a need for document-authentication practices in legal disputes.
pts.d: Bridget McCormack expresses greater concern about deepfake documents than deepfake audio or video because documents feature in almost every dispute. She suggests lawyers consider hashing documents to establish a reference record if authenticity is later contested.

pts.k: McCormack predicts agent-to-agent contracting will generate disputes requiring new expertise and potentially new dispute-resolution options.
pts.d: She describes agents already negotiating contracts, with transactions becoming more complex. She says AAA is preparing new dispute-resolution expertise and considering evidentiary issues, neutral recruitment and education. She also presents AI as a tool for building new dispute-resolution options, without describing a particular deployed solution.

pts.k: McCormack argues human-oriented e-commerce legal infrastructure does not necessarily translate to agentic commerce, potentially obstructing market growth.
pts.d: Her claim concerns contractual formation, consent, authority and records when machines transact rather than humans clicking through terms. She argues legal infrastructure must be designed into the emerging market rather than addressed only after disputes arise.

pts.k: McCormack presents LCP as infrastructure for making contractual terms discoverable and preserving the terms associated with agentic payments.
pts.d: She describes Legal Context Protocol as technology-agnostic, Apache 2.0 licensed and interoperable with other protocols. Its proposed minimum is a known location for legal terms and a hashed record stored with payment. She predicts this will remove uncertainty about the specific terms agreed, while leaving performance, authority and other disputes open. This is her description of the protocol and intended benefits, not a reported evaluation of its effectiveness.

pts.k: McCormack predicts automated contracting mistakes can create substantial exposure at scale, and clearer records can simplify resulting litigation.
pts.d: She illustrates this through a hypothetical manufacturer whose misconfigured procurement agent accepts broad supplier-favouring indemnities in 12,000 transactions over a weekend. In her account, accepting goods and paying invoices produces ratification before humans notice. She predicts mistakes of this kind and argues upfront attention to terms and agent authority will make disputes easier to resolve. The scenario is not presented as an actual case or a measured incidence of error.

pts.k: McCormack predicts agentic commerce creates new advisory and legal-infrastructure work for lawyers rather than eliminating their relevance.
pts.d: She identifies opportunities to help clients deploying agents, design transaction safeguards, contribute to standards and make legal principles machine-readable. She says payments companies, banks and frontier-model companies are developing the market largely without lawyers so far. Her prediction concerns emerging work, not quantified employment growth or a finding that no existing legal work will be displaced.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The claims rest principally on McCormack’s institutional experience, protocol-development work, conceptual papers and an illustrative hypothetical.
pts.d: McCormack cites observing the agentic-commerce market, governance discussions at Legalweek, collaboration with Integra Ledger CEO David Fisher, a trust-problem paper with Fisher and a paper with contracts professor Dave Hoffman on doctrinal gaps. She reports meetings with in-house teams at payments and technology companies. She invokes AAA’s century of experience and more than nine million disputes as support for its convening credibility, not as evidence of LCP outcomes. No measured agent error rates, controlled studies, benchmarks or actual agent-contract litigation outcomes are supplied; document-fabrication and new-work claims are likewise qualitative.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: McCormack urges action now as agentic commerce develops, while leaving future adoption and legal-work growth undated.
pts.d: In the supplied 2026 transcript, she describes agent contracting as already occurring, LCP as an evolving starting point and AAA’s expertise-building as underway. She urges lawyers to examine risks today rather than next year. Community agreement on protocol scope, wider contributions and eventual donation to the Linux Foundation remain prospective; no adoption deadline or quantified market forecast is given.

pts.k: LCP’s predicted benefits are limited to legal-term discoverability and records, not model reliability, valid authority or mandatory dispute-resolution clauses.
pts.d: McCormack explicitly declines to predict whether agents will make more, fewer or more consequential mistakes than humans. LCP is intended to work regardless of model quality and does not remedy hallucinations or other AI inadequacies. Dispute-resolution provisions are optional additions. The practical importance of preserving legal terms arises when an agreement encounters a problem.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: Corporate legal departments, law-firm advisers, dispute-resolution providers and agent-using counterparties face new responsibilities and risks.
pts.d: McCormack advises GCs and law-firm partners to inventory agent use, review form contracts for machine-mediated formation and performance, and monitor or contribute to protocols. Corporate exposure extends across procurement, customer service and marketing; examples also include consumers booking travel and individuals selling through online marketplaces. AAA and its neutrals may need new expertise, education and dispute options. Payments companies, banks, technology platforms and sellers help shape the infrastructure. She identifies an opportunity for lawyers to become proactive designers of safeguards rather than solely responding to failures.
